extracted.intended_audience: correspondents and readers interested in constitutional design and contemporary politics (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Jefferson's criteria and normative judgments for assessing the new U.S. federal Constitution and recommending amendments (notably a declaration of rights, limits on executive re-eligibility, trial by jury, and restraints on standing armies). These are expressed in letters discussing what features are commendable and what defects should be remedied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of the government
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval of the consolidation of the government as a positive feature of the new constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson states he 'approved, from the first moment, of the great mass of what is in the new constitution; the consolidation of the government' — treating consolidation as a criterion of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization into executive, legislative, and judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution's clear organization into three branches is a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson approves 'the organization into executive, legislative, and judiciary' as foundational structure; implies that clear separation and defined departments are essential evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature being subdivided (bicameralism) is a positive design feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He praises 'the subdivision of the legislative' as part of the constitution's merits; the arrangement of legislative bodies and their differing modes of voting is treated as important to balance interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromise between large and small states (different voting in houses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A happy compromise of interests between great and little States by providing different manners of voting in different Houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson highlights the compromise (different voting rules in separate Houses) as a criterion — stability and fairness between constituent states is a measure of constitutional quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting by persons rather than by States
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for voting 'by persons instead of States' in at least some branches as a positive attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson explicitly lists 'the voting by persons instead of States' among features he approved; indicates a criterion favoring individual representation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified negative (executive veto) on laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting a qualified negative (veto) on laws to the executive is a beneficial provision; he would have preferred the judiciary share a similar power as in New York.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He approves 'the qualified negative on laws given to the executive,' but notes a preference that such a negative be 'associated with the judiciary also, as in New York.' This expresses a design criterion about checks and balances across branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of taxation included
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of power of taxation in the federal government is a positive, necessary power (initially thought might be limited, but later judged appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson remarks on 'the power of taxation' as one of the elements he approved; his commentary shows the evaluative question of whether taxation authority should be limited but concludes it ought not to be limited in the instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a declaration (bill) of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration of rights should be annexed to the Constitution to guard liberty against legislative and executive branches and to secure specific individual rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson lists specific rights the declaration should secure: 'freedom in religion, freedom of the press, freedom from monopolies, freedom from unlawful imprisonment, freedom from a permanent military, and a trial by jury, in all cases determinable by the laws of the land.' He argues the declaration provides a legal check for the judiciary, supplies principles for subordinate governments to test federal acts, and is 'a brace' better than nothing. Objections are addressed: even imperfect declarations are valuable ('Half a loaf is better than no bread'). He contrasts temporary inconveniences of a declaration with the permanent evils of lacking one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of rights as judicial/legal check
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration of rights functions as a text by which the judiciary and subordinate governments can try acts of the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson emphasizes the declaration's role in furnishing principles 'whereon to found their opposition' by subordinate governments and as a 'text, whereby they will try all the acts of the federal government.' This is guidance on the practical, institutional purpose of a bill of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury should be secured
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials by jury should be established in all cases determinable by the laws of the land and protected by the declaration of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson insists 'a trial by jury, in all cases determinable by the laws of the land' is among the rights needing explicit security; he notes the new constitution did not secure this adequately and that its absence is a defect to be remedied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict dangerous instruments (standing army) to well-defined cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments especially dangerous to rights (e.g., a standing army) should be restrained and permitted only in well-defined cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson warns that 'There are instruments so dangerous to the rights of the nation... Such an instrument is a standing army. We are now allowed to say, such a declaration of rights... is wanting, to secure us in these points.' This provides a criterion to limit permanent coercive institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual re-eligibility of the President is a defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual re-eligibility of the President is disapproved as a constitutional defect (though Jefferson concedes practical tolerance while Washington remains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson states 'I disapproved, also, the perpetual re-eligibility of the President' and explains his position: although he objects, he would tolerate it temporarily for Washington's service. This gives a normative rule against indefinite executive tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical politics and timing matter for constitutional amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic acceptance or postponement of changes (e.g., tolerating certain provisions now in order to secure the greater good and later amend when feasible) is a pragmatic criterion for constitutional change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson describes preferring that nine conventions accept the constitution and the four later reject it to obtain amendments, then acknowledges a better plan (Massachusetts approach) — signaling that when and how to pursue amendments is itself an evaluative consideration.
